## Building Your Own AI Reviewer (Three Tiers) {#sec-building-reviewer}

Priya now knows the failure modes. She also knows the three levels at which reviewers use AI. Her goal is to build [three tiers]{style="color: #B45309;"} of AI reviewer that she can run locally from Cursor, each addressing progressively more failure modes. This section provides the architectural blueprint and practical guidance for each tier.

### The Architecture Overview

The three tiers correspond to increasing investment in infrastructure and compute, with each tier compensating for failure modes that simpler approaches miss.

| Tier | What It Does | Failure Modes Addressed | Typical Cost/Paper | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Tier 1: Zero-Shot** | Single LLM call with a structured review prompt | Genericness (partially), writing quality, basic structure | $0.05-0.50 | 1-3 min |
| **Tier 2: RAG-Augmented** | Adds retrieval of related papers to the review prompt | Novelty blindness, missing baselines, related work gaps | $0.50-3.00 | 5-15 min |
| **Tier 3: Deep Research** | Multi-agent system with tools, iteration, and literature grounding | All failure modes (to varying degrees) | $3.00-15.00 | 15-60 min |

### Tier 1: Zero-Shot World Knowledge Reviewer

The simplest approach: send the full paper text to a strong LLM with a structured review prompt that mirrors conference review criteria. Russ Poldrack built exactly this with his `ai-peer-review` tool, which sends a paper to six LLMs in parallel (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek R1, and others), collects their reviews, and feeds all anonymized reviews to a single model for meta-review synthesis ([Poldrack, ai-peer-review](https://github.com/poldrack/ai-peer-review); [Poldrack, "Reviewing Scientific Papers with AI: Part 3," Substack 2025](https://russpoldrack.substack.com/p/reviewing-scientific-papers-with-29f)). The entire codebase was generated by Claude Code in 21 minutes, with 836 lines of code, for $0.30 in API charges.

The design pattern is straightforward: (a) parse the PDF to text, (b) construct a system prompt that includes the conference review criteria (soundness, significance, clarity, novelty, reproducibility), (c) send the full paper plus system prompt to each model, (d) collect free-form review outputs, (e) aggregate into a meta-review that highlights concerns raised by multiple models. The ensemble approach adds robustness: if three of six models flag the same weakness, it is probably real.

**What Tier 1 catches:** Surface-level writing issues. Missing sections. Unclear explanations. Basic logical inconsistencies within a paragraph. Claims that contradict well-known facts in the LLM's training data.

**What Tier 1 misses:** Everything documented in @sec-failure-modes. Novelty is not assessed against the actual literature. Figures and tables are not cross-checked against text (most models receive text-only input). The review will be polite, structured, and generic.

**Running in Cursor:** Install the `ai-peer-review` package, configure API keys for your preferred models, and run `ai-peer-review review paper.pdf`. The meta-review output gives you the highest signal-to-noise ratio.

::: {.callout-note title="Think Hard: Is a multi-model ensemble better than a single strong model?"}
Poldrack's approach sends the paper to six models and aggregates. The intuition is that different models have different blind spots, so an ensemble should catch more issues than any single model. This is likely true for breadth (more issues flagged) but not necessarily for depth (quality of individual comments). The MARG paper found that multi-agent *decomposition* (splitting the paper into chunks with specialized agents) was more effective than multi-model *ensembling* for generating specific, actionable feedback. If you can only choose one approach, Tier 2's structured decomposition likely outperforms Tier 1's model ensemble.
:::

### Tier 2: RAG-Augmented Reviewer

Tier 2 adds retrieval to compensate for the LLM's stale and incomplete knowledge of the literature. The architectural pattern comes from two sources: the MARG system from Allen AI, which decomposes papers across multiple agents, and OpenNovelty's structured extraction and retrieval pipeline.

**MARG** (Multi-Agent Review Generation) addresses the practical problem that scientific papers often exceed LLM context limits ([MARG, Allen AI 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04259)). The system splits a paper into chunks at paragraph boundaries, annotates each with its position and section name, and assigns chunks to separate GPT-4 agents that can communicate with each other. Specialized variant MARG-S adds aspect-specific expert agents for experiments, clarity, and impact. In user studies, MARG-S generated 3.7 "good" comments per paper versus 1.7 for a single-agent baseline and 0.3 for a prior method. Crucially, MARG reduced the fraction of generic comments from 60% to 29%, directly addressing Failure 7.

![MARG multi-agent architecture showing how paper chunks are distributed to communicating agents, with specialized experts for different review aspects. Source: MARG (Allen AI, 2024).](AI Reviewers for Scientific Literature/images/marg-architecture.png){#fig-marg-architecture}

**Building a Tier 2 reviewer yourself** involves three components:

1. **Paper parsing:** Convert the PDF to structured markdown with section headers, equations, tables, and figure captions preserved. Tools like MinerU or marker-pdf handle this.
2. **Related work retrieval:** Extract the paper's key claims and search for related work using the Semantic Scholar API or a local corpus. OpenNovelty's approach works well: extract the core task (a 5-15 word problem description) and claimed contributions, then generate semantic search queries with terminology expansion (e.g., both "reinforcement learning" and "RL") ([OpenNovelty, 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01576)).
3. **Augmented review prompt:** Feed the paper text plus retrieved abstracts to the LLM. The prompt should explicitly ask: "Based on the retrieved related work, does this paper's claimed novelty hold? Are there missing baselines?"

**What Tier 2 adds over Tier 1:** Novelty assessment grounded in actual recent literature. Detection of missing baselines and related work. The ability to say "this approach is similar to [specific paper] from [year], which the authors did not cite."

### Tier 3: Deep Research Reviewer

Tier 3 is a full agentic system that iteratively reads, reasons, retrieves, and validates. The best existing example is DeepReviewer v2, which was published at ACL 2025 ([DeepReviewer v2](https://github.com/ResearAI/DeepReviewer-v2)). Its architecture is a tool-grounded reasoning loop: the review agent can call tools to read specific lines of the paper (`pdf_read_lines`), annotate the PDF with comments (`pdf_annotate`), search for related papers (`paper_search`), and write the final review (`review_final_markdown_write`). The agent decides which tools to call and how many times, with "finalization gates" that require minimum thresholds (at least 3 paper search calls, at least 10 annotations) before allowing the agent to submit the review.

![OpenNovelty's four-phase pipeline for automated novelty assessment: Extract claims from the target paper, retrieve related prior work, analyze overlap, and synthesize a novelty report. Source: OpenNovelty (2026).](AI Reviewers for Scientific Literature/images/opennovelty-pipeline.png){#fig-opennovelty-pipeline}

**Building a Tier 3 reviewer** is substantially more complex than Tiers 1 and 2. The key components are:

1. **An agent framework** that supports iterative tool use (LangChain, LangGraph, or a custom loop)
2. **Paper-reading tools** that let the agent read specific sections on demand rather than ingesting the full paper at once
3. **Literature search tools** connected to Semantic Scholar, arXiv, or Google Scholar APIs
4. **Cross-validation tools** that check claims in the abstract against the results, verify that all cited works exist, and compare figures against the text they describe
5. **A structured output format** that maps to the conference review form (soundness, significance, clarity, novelty, each with justification and evidence)

**What Tier 3 adds over Tier 2:** Iterative reasoning (the agent can go back and re-read sections). Line-level precision (comments reference specific paragraphs). Verifiable novelty assessment with cited prior work. Cross-section consistency checking. The ability to produce a review that includes specific page and line references, something generic AI reviews never do.

### Meta-Review Synthesis

Priya runs all three tiers on her TokenMix paper. Tier 1 flags generic issues (writing clarity in Section 4.2, missing related work citation). Tier 2 identifies a specific paper she missed (a concurrent token-mixing approach from a different lab). Tier 3 catches the planted abstract-results inconsistency and notes that her novelty claim overlaps with two prior methods she did not adequately differentiate from. Following Poldrack's approach, she feeds all three sets of feedback to a single model for synthesis, producing a prioritized list of issues ranked by how many tiers flagged each one.

### Cost and Practical Guidance

| Component | Recommended Tool | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| PDF parsing | MinerU, marker-pdf | Free (local) | MinerU handles layout better |
| Tier 1 review | Claude Opus 4.6 or GPT-5 | $0.10-0.50 per paper | Ensemble 3-6 models for robustness |
| Tier 2 retrieval | Semantic Scholar API | Free (rate-limited) | 100 requests/5 min without key |
| Tier 3 agent loop | DeepReviewer v2 or custom | $3-15 per paper | GPT-5 or Claude for best results |
| Meta-review | Gemini 2.5 Pro | $0.05 | Aggregate and prioritize |

::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: 'Building an AI reviewer requires fine-tuning'"}
None of the three tiers require fine-tuning a model. Tier 1 uses prompt engineering only. Tier 2 adds retrieval augmentation. Tier 3 adds agentic tool use. All three work with off-the-shelf API models. The MARG paper showed that the right architecture (multi-agent decomposition) matters more than the right model. Fine-tuning helps for specific subtasks (like the SEA framework's fine-tuned Mistral-7B for mismatch scoring), but the core review pipeline is entirely prompt-and-tool-based.
:::
